# Clinical Vignette: Miguel

Miguel was twenty-two when the IED detonated forty meters from his Humvee on a supply route outside Kandahar. He remembers the percussion—not a sound but a feeling that moved through his whole body—and then the acrid smell of burning plastic and flesh. He remembers Staff Sergeant Reeves's arm, severed cleanly at the elbow, lying on the sand. He remembers screaming orders that made no sense. He remembers the weight of Reeves's body as they pulled him into the vehicle. What Miguel cannot remember is the order in which these things happened. When he tries to reconstruct that morning, the sequence collapses. Sometimes the arm comes first, sometimes the smell. Sometimes he is outside the Humvee, sometimes inside. The uncertainty of the timeline troubles him more than the events themselves—as if his mind is refusing to file away what occurred into any coherent narrative.

Two years have passed since Miguel was medically discharged. He is now twenty-four, working as a financial analyst for a mid-sized firm in Denver, and the memories have not faded. If anything, they have become more intrusive. Fragments arrive without warning—a sudden flash of Reeves's face, the specific shade of red on sand, the smell of diesel fuel mixed with something charred—and then they vanish just as quickly, leaving Miguel disoriented and gasping. These pieces come most often in the afternoon, around the time the deployment would have been conducting that route. He has learned not to trust his own mind.

What frightens Miguel most now is not the memories themselves but what they mean about him. In the weeks after returning home, he had isolated himself from his family—his mother calling constantly, his younger sister trying to draw him out, his tía insisting he come to Sunday dinner. He avoided them all, not because he was angry but because their presence reminded him of what he had lost in Kandahar. His closest friend from high school, Danny, had been killed in a separate engagement three months into Miguel's deployment. Every time his mother mentioned Danny's name, Miguel felt the grief rising like floodwater, and he could not bear it. So he stopped answering calls. He stopped going home. He told himself it was better this way—that keeping his distance protected them from his presence, from the person he had become.

The person he had become was someone who had made decisions in combat that contradicted everything he believed about himself. Miguel had always considered himself principled, measured, someone who thought carefully about right and wrong. But in those moments of chaos and terror, he had fired on a structure where civilians might have been sheltering. He had done it because his squad was pinned and afraid, because the order came from above, because survival demanded it. He has come to believe that he is fundamentally compromised, that he acted in ways that go against who he is at his core, and that this violation is permanent. No amount of reasoning changes the fact of what his hands did.

At work, Miguel sits in an open-plan office on the fifteenth floor. The exposure of the space—the windows on all sides, the lack of walls, the sense of being visible and unprotected—has become intolerable. He requested a transfer to an interior cubicle, citing a preference for fewer distractions, but the request was denied. Instead, he has begun arriving before dawn and leaving after everyone else, working in the quiet office when he is alone. His productivity has remained strong, but his supervisor has noticed his isolation and has begun to worry. Colleagues invite him to lunch; he declines. The team went out for drinks after closing a major deal; Miguel said he had family obligations and drove home to his apartment, where he sat in the dark.

Three weeks ago, Miguel received a call from his mother. Danny's younger brother had graduated high school and was enlisting in the Marines. His mother was terrified. She wanted Miguel to call the boy, to tell him what combat was really like, to convince him not to go. Miguel could not do it. The thought of speaking about the deployment, of reliving it in words, of making it real in conversation, was unbearable. He told his mother he could not help her. She wept. He hung up.

Yesterday, Miguel made an appointment with a VA therapist. He is certain that his future is already written—that he will never feel whole again, that the person he was before Kandahar is gone forever, and that he will always be an outsider to the people he once loved. But his mother's voice on the phone, breaking as she asked for his help, has made him willing to try. He does not expect to be fixed. He is hoping, against all evidence, that someone might help him understand why he cannot stop remembering, and why the person he has become feels so completely foreign to himself.
